chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Safwan ibn Yahya, who said:

I asked Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the man who swears, and his inner intention (conscience) is upon something other than what he swore upon. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The oath is upon the inner intention (conscience).'
ai.seo_question: How is an oath judged in Shia jurisprudence when the spoken words differ from the inner intention?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the jurisprudential principle that the validity of an oath (yamin) depends on the swearer's inner intention (ضمير) rather than the literal semantics of the words uttered. In Shia fiqh, this establishes that if one swears with a specific meaning in mind, even if the words are ambiguous, the oath is binding according to that intended meaning, prioritizing the heart's resolve over linguistic form. This ruling is crucial for resolving disputes in personal vows and oaths where literal interpretation might contradict the speaker's true intent.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Safwan Bin Yahya who said,
‘I asked Abu Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup> about the man who swore, and his conscience was upon other than what he had sworn upon. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The oath is upon the conscience’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Safwan ibn Yahya who has narrated the following:

“I once asked abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a man who swears but his mind is on something other than that for which he has taken the oath. He (the Imam) said, ‘Swearing is for that which is in one’s mind.’”
